newsitem.title: UK: UK's SFA raps two Merrill staff for breaking rules.
newsitem.headline: UK's SFA raps two Merrill staff for breaking rules.

text.p: UK financial markets watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) said on Thursday that in unrelated cases it had reprimanded and fined two representatives of Merrill Lynch International Bank (MLIB).
The SFA said in a statement it had reprimanded Melville Ipe, a financial consultant with MLIB, fined him 7,500 pounds ($12,660) and ordered him to pay 7,500 pounds towards costs.

It said Ipe had "recommended a transaction to a private customer of MLIB in a structured derivative product without having taken reasonable steps to enable the customer to understand the nature of the risks involved".

The transaction was, it added, "unsuitable for that customer given his investment objectives and attitude to risk". The customer in question was the uncle of one of Ipe's colleagues and his investment objectives were given as "income, growth and total return", the required risk factor as "moderate".

But the term sheets for the investments recommended by Ipe said the instruments had been designed for "sophisticated investors" and contained "interest rate risk". They also included other guidance which showed they were not suitable for the customer in this case, a fact accepted by Ipe, the SFA said.
As a result of the purchase of the notes, the customer sustained a loss of $47,270 when they were sold. He has been compensated in full by MLIB, including $15,000 from Ipe.
"He (Ipe) accepts full responsibility for his actions, has admitted he was at fault and has resolved not to repeat similar misconduct in the future," the SFA said.

The second, unrelated case was against Tanvier Malik, a former registered representative of MLIB, who has been reprimanded, fined 15,000 pounds and ordered to pay 5,000 pounds towards costs, the SFA said.
It said that while employed by MLIB Malik had provided four incomplete valuation reports to a private customer for whom the firm was managing a discretionary portfolio.

"Four transactions, which were omitted, were all loss-making foreign exchange transactions, whose exclusion from the valuations caused a seriously misleading impression of the customer's portfolio," it added.

Malik also failed to take reasonable steps to ensure that sufficient information was recorded by MLIB correctly classifying his customer and he has admitted that he operated the account on a discretionary basis, without the permission or knowledge of his employers.

The SFA said Malik explained that the first valuation was provided by him "under intense pressure from the customer and omitted the forex transactions by accident". Three subsequent valuations repeated the omission as Malik was "frightened to disclose that he made the initial error".

"Malik has admitted that he acted stupidly, but without dishonest intent, in providing the incorrect valuations. He made no personal gain (and) has expressed deep regret for his actions," the SFA said.
